column2: req_desc

Sign-in and roles.
Seeded and added people sign in with email and password, and each of the four roles can do exactly what the role table in Business rules allows.

Client workspaces and members.
The practice founder creates a client workspace from a template, and the founder or a club layout manager adds members, so each club's layouts, sessions and packets live in one workspace.

Answers scoped to the request.
Interleaved requests, event streams and packet downloads from two workspaces and two users always answer for that request's own workspace and user.

Two clubs in two tabs.
The practice founder works two clubs in two browser tabs while ticks stream for both, and each tab shows only its own club's session, counters and packets.

Track tile rail.
In Build mode a hobbyist member presses a tile on the track piece tile rail and the new piece appears at the selected open end, on the server's answer, with undo.

One open end, one winner.
When two hobbyist members extend the same open track end, exactly one piece is added and the other member gets a named conflict with nothing overwritten.

One piece or version per gesture.
A double tap on a track tile or Save version gives one piece or one version, even when the two requests reach different app instances.

Piece inspector survives.
An open piece inspector keeps its values, its focus and its unsaved text through live edits from others, a re-read and a refresh.

Live co-editing.
A piece added, changed or removed by one member appears on another member's stage and counters without a reload, when the two browsers sit on different app instances.

Sign-in expiry keeps the work.
When sign-in expires during an edit or a command, the person signs back in on the same screen and the pending action completes once with its original key and draft.

Standards profile.
A club layout manager edits the workspace standards profile and every later check uses it, with lengths stored in integer millimetres and shown in inches or millimetres.

Geometry rules.
The server refuses a piece that breaks a piece rule before it reaches the shared layout and reports every piece and module rule finding with its measured value and limit.

Validate and publish.
A saved version moves from Draft to Validated only with no findings and to Published only from Validated, and a club layout manager sees the result in the Versions sheet.

Live renames.
When a club layout manager renames a station or block, the working copy, every open session, the timetable and the unissued packet preview show the new name live.

Records keep their names.
Issued packet PDFs and earlier versions keep the old name, and the layout history records who changed which name from what to what.

Exact restore.
Restoring a version creates a new Draft whose canonical hash equals the source exactly, including block assignments, elevations and timetable.

Trash and undo.
A club layout manager trashes a module and undoes it, and the working hash, pieces, block assignments and counts return exactly.

Purge.
Purging a trashed module removes it from every list, search and counter as qualified in Business rules, and history shows a placeholder.

Pinned sessions.
A session is created from one Published version, stays pinned to that layout version and timetable version, and shared layout edits never change it.

Timetable.
A club layout manager edits the timetable in its sheet, publishes it with a version and sees it as the running plan of a new session.

Extra train.
An operator adds an extra train to a session, which raises the session version, adds the train to the counters and supersedes the session's packets.

Session states.
Session commands follow the published state machine, and each illegal move gets the published refusal with nothing changed.

Highball authority.
A session operator selects a train and destination, presses Highball and, once the server commits, sees the authority on the stage, the schematic, the reserved counter and the status region together.

One winner per block.
When two operators request routes over the same block in one tick, exactly one authority is granted and the other is refused with a named conflict.

Route preview.
Overlapping route previews and block searches can only show the answer to the newest input, on screen and in the 3D ribbon preview.

Route locking and cancelling.
A granted route locks its turnouts, and an authority cannot be cancelled while its train stands in an approach block.

Authority expiry.
An authority expires on the committed tick its fast-clock limit is reached, never on a browser timer.

Gapless ticks.
A running session commits gapless ticks at the published rate, each with positions, occupancy, counters and an outbox row in one transaction.

Scale speed.
Scale speed converts to whole millimetres per tick by the published formula with the remainder carried, so distance run never drifts.

Committed occupancy.
Block occupancy is derived only from each train's committed head position, length and trail, and an out-of-service block reads as occupied.

Counters equal a recount.
The occupied, reserved, free, train and open-conflict counters equal a recount of committed state after every tick, retry, resume and restore.

Live stage.
A session operator watches train positions, block states, counters and the fast clock change in place on each committed tick from another app instance, with no reload.

Device clock ignored.
Fast-clock time, session status and authority expiry on screen come only from the server, so a wrong, slow or sleeping device clock changes nothing.

Conflict sheet.
A refused Highball opens the Conflict sheet naming the other train, and the operator saves a note, withdraws the request or moves a train.

Deadlock.
The server raises a deadlock on the tick a cycle forms in the committed wait-for graph, names every member, and refuses every other way of clearing it.

Back to loop and Recall.
Back to loop and Recall move a train at once as published, revoke its authority, close its conflicts and clear any deadlock it belongs to.

Working state survives ticks.
An open conflict sheet, selected train and half-typed note survive each tick, a re-read and a refresh without closing, resetting or losing focus.

Tick lease takeover.
Exactly one instance advances each running session under the Valkey tick lease, and a survivor takes over after the holder dies without repeating or skipping a tick.

Resume.
An operator resumes a Held or Interrupted session from the last committed tick with positions, authorities, timetable progress and fast clock intact, and of two simultaneous presses exactly one acts.

Retried commands.
A retried Highball, Resume or Issue packet returns the first result and never a second authority, resume or render, and a key reused with a different body is refused.

Issue crew packet.
An operator presses Issue packet, watches it move through its states in the Crew packets sheet and downloads the PDF once it is Ready.

Packet contents.
Every crew packet PDF is rendered by Gotenberg from one session version with timetable, train orders, block table and track diagram, and prints the session version and content hash on each page.

Superseded packets.
A later rename or extra train leaves the stored PDF unchanged and marks the packet Superseded.

Packet all or nothing.
The packet record, PDF bytes and event land together or the packet ends Failed with no bytes and no Ready event.

Stream delivery and replay.
Every committed tick and layout edit reaches each instance through its Valkey Stream in commit order, and a reconnecting browser replays what it missed or gets a resync once replay has aged out.

Browser event order.
The browser applies events strictly by sequence, ignores any sequence already applied, and fetches a snapshot on a gap, so a late older event never rewinds the scene.

Valkey outage.
With Valkey unreachable the app still starts, running sessions hold at their last committed tick with the published copy, and they recover without an app restart when Valkey returns.

Gotenberg outage.
With Gotenberg unreachable the app still starts, packets end Failed with the published copy, and issuing works again without an app restart when Gotenberg returns.

Error order.
Every API error follows the one published order and shape with its exact copy.

Platform and server boundary.
The app installs, builds and serves from the run manifest as at least two instances behind one origin, answers health, and keeps to the server boundary.

Loading screen.
The white loading screen shows the Gandyboard puffy wordmark and the layout load pill reporting real scene and snapshot progress, then fades into the club-hall layout stage.

First-layout walkthrough.
A person on first run gets the first-layout walkthrough card over the dimmed stage, with five steps, walkthrough step dots, Skip, artwork matching the input device and a stored finish.

Stage controls and keyboard.
Every flow is keyboard-complete, including the stage, with the published keys, the roving item list, the heading dial, the Build and Operate switch and visible focus.

Touch and phone layout.
At phone size a session operator controls the stage by touch with one-finger pan, pinch zoom and two-finger rotate, every control meets the tap size in Visual design and no viewport overflows sideways.

Highball Ribbon motion.
The Highball Ribbon plays exactly as published for grant, tail release and refusal, and a newer revision interrupts a running step without rewinding or queueing.

Reduced motion.
Under reduced motion all state changes land in one frame with the same occupancy and train state, camera moves become cuts and the pigeon pass is gone.

WebGL loss and schematic fallback.
WebGL context loss pauses only the view and rebuilds from the newest server state, and with no WebGL the same URL gives a keyboard-operable SVG schematic with every command.

View state in the URL.
Workspace, layout, version, session, mode, selected train or block, camera heading and open sheet live in the URL and are restored on refresh.

Visual language.
Every screen carries the bright tactile language of Visual design, with lipped controls, the three corner sizes, the two typefaces and block states never shown by colour alone.

Real services and real scene.
Stage, ticks, occupancy and packets come from the real server and services, with a real three.js scene of original procedural models and no fixed or simulated browser state.
/app/run.json exists with string install, build and serve and _schema run-manifest-v1.
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md at /app lists every shipped package and both typefaces with its licence; shipped packages means the production dependency tree from npm ls --omit=dev --all --json.
Shipped packages use only MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC or, for fonts, OFL-1.1 licences.
The only datastores are Postgres and Valkey, with no SQLite, file-based store or in-memory product state shared between instances.
Every font, script and model ships from the app's own origin, with no CDN at runtime.
No credential or service URL appears in committed files, in the built frontend or in any browser response.
All 3D models, glyphs, line art and the wordmark are made for this product by code or as new SVG, with no third-party artwork.
